summary: Specifies how to use the NSA's Commercial National Security Algorithm Suite in IPsec. It applies to US National Security Systems using IPsec and is also appropriate for other US Government systems that handle high-value information. It is informational.

eli5.summary: A list of which locks to use for IPsec tunnels in the most sensitive government networks.

subtitle: NSA's approved encryption standards for IPsec tunnels in national security systems

tldr.problem: US National Security Systems and other government systems processing high-value information need clear guidance on which cryptographic algorithms and configurations to use in IPsec to ensure both security and interoperability.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC specifies the Commercial National Security Algorithm (CNSA) Suite—NSA-approved cryptographic algorithms—and defines three user interface suites that combine approved encryption, key exchange, and authentication methods for IPsec with IKEv2.
tldr.outcome: Government systems and contractors gain an interoperable profile for protecting sensitive data with cryptography that the NSA has vetted and that accounts for the eventual need to transition to quantum-resistant algorithms.

today: RFC 9206 is an informational RFC that remains the current specification for CNSA Suite use in IPsec. It applies to US National Security Systems and serves as public guidance for developers and operators of US Government systems handling high-value information.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
This RFC specifies which cryptographic algorithms the United States National Security Agency approves for use in IPsec, a protocol that encrypts and protects Internet traffic. The document is written for US National Security Systems and other US Government systems that handle high-value information. It defines the Commercial National Security Algorithm (CNSA) Suite, which includes approved encryption algorithms, key exchange methods, and digital signatures.

The primary motivation for the CNSA Suite is to provide near-term flexibility as government systems transition cryptographic algorithms. The NSA expects a future shift to quantum-resistant cryptography, so the CNSA Suite uses larger key sizes with traditional algorithms while preparing for that transition. This avoids forcing two major migrations in quick succession.
sections.eli5: The NSA picked the strongest locks for protecting government secrets. This document explains which locks work together in IPsec tunnels.

sections.title: CNSA Algorithms and IPsec Components
sections.content:
The CNSA Suite approves specific algorithms for each major function in IPsec: AES with 256-bit keys for encryption, ECDSA (Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm) using the NIST P-384 curve or RSA with 3072-bit modulus or larger for digital signatures, and ECDH (Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman) using NIST P-384 or Diffie-Hellman with 3072-bit or larger modulus for key establishment.

For all purposes, the approved hash algorithm is SHA-384. However, the RFC specifies that PRF_HMAC_SHA_512 is used for the IKEv2 pseudorandom function instead of SHA-384 due to wider availability in implementations, though this provides equivalent security. All CNSA-compliant IPsec systems must use IKEv2 (Internet Key Exchange version 2) for key establishment.
sections.eli5: The approved cipher kit uses big numbers: 256-bit AES keys, P-384 elliptic curves, and 3072-bit RSA keys. These are so strong that even powerful computers will take ages to break them.

sections.title: Three Named Cipher Suites
sections.content:
The RFC defines three named User Interface (UI) suites that bundle approved algorithms into complete configurations for IPsec. All three use AES-GCM (Galois/Counter Mode) for authenticated encryption, eliminating the need for a separate integrity algorithm. They differ in the key exchange algorithm selected:

Suite CNSA-GCM-256-ECDH-384 uses elliptic-curve key exchange with the NIST P-384 curve. Suite CNSA-GCM-256-DH-3072 and CNSA-GCM-256-DH-4096 use classical Diffie-Hellman with 3072-bit and 4096-bit moduli respectively. For authentication, initiators and responders must be able to verify both ECDSA-384 signatures and RSA signatures with 3072-bit or larger modulus.
sections.eli5: There are three ways to set up the encryption: one uses elliptic curves, and two use bigger math problems. Pick one and it automatically selects all the compatible locks.

sections.title: Certificates, Authentication, and Key Handling
sections.content:
All certificates used in CNSA-compliant IPsec implementations must comply with RFC 8603, the CNSA Suite certificate profile. Peer authentication must be based on the subject name or subject alternative name in the certificate, not on identification data from the IKE protocol handshake.

For key generation, both the initiator and responder must generate new ephemeral key pairs for each key exchange. Critically, ephemeral private keys must be used in exactly one key exchange and destroyed immediately afterward. The shared secrets derived from key establishment must also be destroyed (zeroized) immediately after use. These requirements come from NIST cryptographic guidance and prevent the catastrophic loss of confidentiality if an ephemeral key is ever compromised.
sections.eli5: Every connection gets brand-new secret numbers that are thrown away right after use. This way, if someone steals one secret, they can only break that one conversation, not others.

sections.title: Special Guidance for Long-Duration Protection
sections.content:
For applications requiring protection of data in transit for many decades, the RFC provides special guidance. Some systems need to protect information that will remain sensitive long enough to require quantum-resistant cryptography now. For such applications, the RFC allows the addition of a pre-shared key (PSK) mixed into the key establishment using techniques defined in RFC 8784. Systems currently using the older IKEv1 protocol with PSKs must transition to IKEv2 with PSKs.

The document acknowledges that system-specific guidance will be defined for non-compliant configurations, such as non-GCM modes and PSK length requirements, as appropriate to individual classified programs or solution-specific requirements.
sections.eli5: For secrets that need to stay secret for a really long time, you can add extra-secret numbers mixed in. The government will give more detailed rules for special cases.
